claims.text: The initial material is an equiatomic high-entropy alloy.
The target HEAs are single-phase and chemically disordered, with an FCC or BCC structure and significant lattice distortion.
A model quantifying atomic-scale local lattice distortion and mass variance will identify exceptionally low-phonon-conductivity HEAs more accurately than conventional averaging models.
The proposed method integrates computed local strain fields, atomic-mass variance, and chemical-disorder descriptors into a machine-learning model.
Well-annealed samples measured at ambient pressure and temperature will have minimized extrinsic contributions to thermal transport.
Under the specified conditions, intrinsic phonon transport and lattice scattering will dominate.
Local lattice distortion and heterogeneous atomic masses induce strong phonon scattering.
Chemical disorder disrupts phonon dispersion and enhances phonon scattering.
Detailed atomistic descriptors capture phonon-scattering behavior that is missed by averaged material parameters.
Capturing atomistic disorder enables the model to pinpoint alloys with substantially reduced phonon mean free paths.
HEAs selected by the proposed approach will exhibit phonon thermal conductivity at least 20–30% below values predicted by conventional averaging models.
The conventional baseline estimates alloy thermal conductivity using averaged atomic mass and bonding parameters.
The proposed approach is primarily applicable to single-phase, disordered HEAs.
Significant secondary phases or chemical ordering may introduce alternative phonon-conduction pathways and limit the approach.
Direct experimental measurements of phonon thermal conductivity in HEAs are limited.
Local lattice effects may be difficult to quantify reliably.
Candidate HEAs selected by the advanced and conventional models will be synthesized, structurally characterized, and tested for phonon thermal conductivity.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant 20–30% reduction relative to conventional-model predictions is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.
